newsitem.title: USA: Clinton defends fund raising, deplores system.
newsitem.headline: Clinton defends fund raising, deplores system.

text.p: A combative President Bill Clinton defended controversial campaign fund-raising practices on Friday, saying he and his subordinates broke no laws and that the fault lay in an "out of whack" political system.

At a news conference where he was bombarded with questions on the issue, Clinton also said he could not say definitively whether he himself did or did not solicit campaign donations by telephone from the White House, a practice that has opened Vice President Al Gore to criticism.

"I can't say that over all the hundreds and hundreds, maybe thousands of phone calls I've made in the past four years, that I never said to anybody while I was talking to them, 'well, we need your help,' or 'I hope you'll help us,'" Clinton said.

But he stood his ground during an unusually long session of 51 minutes as questioner after questioner suggested the White House had acted improperly if not illegally in raising tens of millions of dollars for his 1996 re-election campaign.
White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles said later that Clinton was relaxed and calm after the grilling.
"He felt good ... I think he was pleased with this press conference," Bowles said on CNN's "Larry King Live."

The Democratic president told reporters he and his aides wanted to be competitive with a well-heeled Republican Party that consistently outspends the Democrats, and were operating in a campaign environment that gobbles money.
"I don't think there's something intrinsically bad (about fund raising) but the system is out of whack," he said, renewing his call for campaign finance reform legislation.

Clinton rejected suggestions that Gore erred in soliciting campaign funds by telephone from his White House office. And he was emphatic in defending his wife's chief of staff, Maggie Williams, who is in hot water for having accepted $50,000 from a campaign donor with Asian ties in the White House despite a law forbidding such activity on federal property.

"She is an honourable person," he said, conceding that, in retrospect, it would have been wiser for Williams to ask the donor to give the check to the Democratic National Committee instead of using her as a go-between.

Congressional Republicans are preparing to set up a Senate investigation into the fund-raising controversy. They are also demanding that Attorney General Janet Reno appoint an independent counsel to run a separate probe that could lead to criminal prosecutions of any wrongdoing alleged -- a move that Clinton said was unjustified.

"I do not believe there's anything wrong for a president, me or anyone else, reaching out to his supporters," he said. "I don't think you can find any evidence of the fact that I changed government policy solely because of a contribution," he added, referring to Republican charges the Democrats accepted money from Asian business interests and others who sought to influence U.S. policy.

Clinton's Democratic Party has returned nearly $3 million to donors -- most of them men with links to Asian businesses or governments -- that were deemed illegal or questionable. This, and a lack of background checks on some contributors and friends of contributors who gained access to the White House, brought Clinton's only expression of dismay.
He said he was "livid and stunned" that his party had not made sure the contributions were proper before accepting them. "It took my breath away," he said.
Clinton also said he had wrongly assumed that everyone who entered the White House underwent longstanding screening procedures and had acted to correct the situation.
